source.title: Decoding Dense Embeddings: Sparse Autoencoders for Interpreting and Discretizing Dense Retrieval
source.authors: Seongwan Park; Tae-Kyung Kim; Youngjoong Ko

record.file_problem: none; full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study argues that standard-basis dimensions can be polysemantic and reports a latent-intrusion comparison in which SimLM’s 768-dimensional representation scores below SAE latents. This challenges the broader idea that individual neurons/dimensions are reliably interpretable, but it does not test any version’s specified audit, model scope, circuit attribution, or explanation-scoring measure.
record.gate_note: The relevant result is Appendix G’s latent-intrusion comparison of SimLM’s standard-basis hidden representation and SAE latents. The paper does not report a neuron-pole share or test the claim versions’ specified conditions. Other SAE reconstruction, retrieval, and human-interpretation results concern different measures; cited claims about neurons are not study results.
record.test_reason: This is a sparse-autoencoder method paper for a dense retrieval encoder (SimLM). It cites neuron polysemanticity (Olah 2020, superposition) as motivation and reports its own method's performance. Its one neuron-related result (Appendix G) runs a latent-intrusion test on SimLM's 768 output-embedding dimensions: 0.46, versus 0.86 for its SAE latents. That is an own-method comparison on a proxy task. It concerns embedding coordinates of a retrieval encoder, not MLP neuron poles. It reports no share of neurons with one or two jobs, no scale or architecture comparison, no attribution graphs, and no simulation scoring. So it bears on no version as stated.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase overweights an appendix aside. The authors' main conclusion is that SAEs decompose DPR dense embeddings into interpretable latent concepts that preserve retrieval information. They report high human-interpretability accuracy (0.90–0.94) and that CL-SR built on these latents matches neural sparse retrievers more efficiently and robustly. In Appendix G they say they believe standard-basis dimensions are polysemantic in this setting, citing Olah 2020. They support this with an intrusion accuracy of 0.46 versus 0.86 for SAE latents.
record.recipe_differences: The comparison uses a latent-intrusion accuracy test on SimLM’s standard-basis representation and SAE latents, rather than auditing neuron poles and estimating their job-count shares. The target is a dense retrieval encoder, not Qwen3-32B.

fits_no_version.finding: On SimLM's 768-dim output embedding, a GPT-4.1-mini latent-intrusion test (9 top passages plus 1 intruder) scores 0.46 for standard-basis dimensions versus 0.86 for k=32 BatchTopK SAE latents.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a dense retrieval encoder's output embedding, standard-basis dimensions are less coherent on an LLM-judged intrusion test than SAE latents.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The relevant neuron-versus-SAE comparison is reported for one dense retrieval model and one interpretability proxy task. No uncertainty estimate or explicit chance/control result is stated for that comparison; the task score does not directly measure whether dimensions predict model behavior on new inputs.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were extracted: the paper’s reconstruction, retrieval, and human interpretability results do not measure neuron-pole interpretability or any named version’s outcome. Cited statements about neuron polysemanticity are not study results.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B audit and no classification of neuron poles into one-job, two-job or unexplained shares.
No neuron-share measurements across language models, dense or MoE, or across scale. SimLM embedding dimensions are not neurons audited for job counts.
No InceptionV1 or canonical polysemantic neuron re-analysis.
No manipulation of architecture, regularization or tools, and no measure of the interpretable-neuron share as tools improve.
No neuron-based attribution graphs and no comparison with replacement models.
No test of whether explanations from activating examples predict firing on new inputs, for neurons.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T5/tests guess is rejected. The neuron comparison is an own-method baseline on embedding coordinates of a BERT-style retriever, and it is judged by one LLM with no chance or control stated. At most it is weak context for the superposition view, not a test of any version.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit Qwen3-32B, classify positive/negative neuron poles, or report the stated proportions.
Does not measure the stated shares across language-model sizes, dense and MoE architectures, or trillion-parameter models.
Does not examine InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose, or recursive generalization.
Does not test architecture, regularization, tool quality, or the stated InceptionV1-sized model estimates.
Does not construct attribution graphs or test whether model behavior can be explained using its own neurons without a replacement model.
Does not test whether explanations from activating examples predict where a neuron fires.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulating their activations on new text.

rows.subject: SimLM
rows.operation_detail: Measured accuracy on a latent-intrusion task using the standard-basis hidden representation.
rows.locator: Appendix G, Comparison with Neuron-based Interpretability
rows.note: The paper compares this standard-basis result with its SAE-based method and interprets the lower accuracy as evidence of poorer interpretability. This is not a measurement of the proportion of individual neuron poles with one or more jobs.
rows.check: The subject is SimLM's final 768-dim output embedding coordinates (standard basis), not MLP neurons or neuron poles. Intrusion accuracy over all dimensions, with no chance or control reported (chance about 0.10 for 1-of-10), cannot give a per-neuron share of single-job neurons. It is a related construct only.

rows.subject: SimLM
rows.size_stated: 768-dimensional hidden representation as the comparison setting; SAE latent count not stated here
rows.operation_detail: Measured accuracy on the same latent-intrusion task using SAE-based latents.
rows.locator: Appendix G, Comparison with Neuron-based Interpretability
rows.note: Comparator to the standard-basis representation; the paper reports 0.86 here, while Table 2 reports 0.859 for SAE k=32 under the latent intrusion test.
rows.check: This is the study's own SAE method, used as a comparator to the standard basis. It is an own-method performance value and should not be a result row on any version. The 0.86 here matches Table 2's 0.859 for k=32.
